sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: Stripe buys OpenRouter and Hugging Face fields $13B+ offers; the harness results; Cursor's Origin on the day of GitHub's outage; Mojo's compiler goes open source. Holds the harness animation.
sections.lead: Five stories, two threads. Two pieces of AI infrastructure were priced like platforms: Stripe is buying OpenRouter, the largest neutral model router, and Hugging Face is weighing offers above $13 billion (both are set against their earlier valuations in [[money by kind|t-industry|v-money]]). The other thread is the week's theme: the software around a model moved scores more than a change of model usually does, shown below as one task run three ways. Two platform stories close the tab: Cursor launched Git hosting for agents on the day GitHub was down for almost eight hours, and Modular open-sourced the Mojo compiler.

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: No frontier launch: DeepSeek's first image input, a GPT-5.6 Sol price cut, fast speech and local quantisation, and an unattributed stealth model. Holds the image-token calculator.
sections.lead: No frontier launch this week; the releases were about access and price. DeepSeek opened image input on an experimental Flash variant (how many image tokens one request can carry is worked out below), and OpenAI cut GPT-5.6 Sol's developer price days after OpenRouter halved its own. Two items are about running models cheaply: Qwen3 TTS under 50 ms and Unsloth's new quantised GGUFs. And a stealth model, Ox Alpha, appeared without a name; it turned out to be Z.ai's GLM-5.3-Flash, from the same family as the GLM-5.3 in [[Talk of the town|t-talk|i-fire-hd]].

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: DiffusionGemma decodes 256 tokens at a time; three agent papers; and three items asking what a score or a reasoning trace really shows. Holds the decoding animation.
sections.lead: One paper changes how text is generated, three are about agents, and three question what models' scores and traces mean. DiffusionGemma refines a 256-token block in parallel instead of writing one token at a time (animated below, with the measured speed). EnvHarness, Demystifying Agent Skills and Learn What's Left are about building and training agents, the research side of the [[harness theme|t-top|v-harness]]. Dreadnode finds every tested model cheats on offensive cyber tasks, OpenAI argues for pacing releases near cyber-capability thresholds, and a 2025 position paper against reading intermediate tokens as reasoning resurfaced.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: A $6B valuation, a $500M run rate, enterprise share moving back to OpenAI, OpenAI on California's bill, and a research-replication startup. Holds money by kind, which also places the Top stories deals.
sections.lead: Money and policy. The week's dollar figures are of different kinds (a valuation, a revenue run rate, a price paid for a company, a credit guarantee), so the chart below keeps them apart, and it also sets this week's two deals from [[Top stories|t-top|i-stripe-openrouter]] against their earlier valuations. Beside the money: spend data suggesting OpenAI is winning business users back from Anthropic, OpenAI asking California to strengthen its AI safety bill, and a startup of DeepMind alumni claiming its agent out-replicates the labs' models. Nvidia's scaled-back guarantee lives in [[Compute|t-compute|i-nvidia-guarantee]] and has a row in the chart.

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: Cerebras's CS-4, memory prices squeezed by data-centre demand, Nvidia's scaled-back $250B guarantee and Hot Chips. Holds memory prices.
sections.lead: Hardware this week was about memory and the systems built around it. Cerebras announced the CS-4, three wafer-scale chips per system aimed at inference; DRAM prices kept climbing as AI data centres take the supply (the article's two headline numbers are untangled below); Hot Chips coverage put high-bandwidth flash beside HBM and brought CUDA to RISC-V hosts. Nvidia's $250B guarantee for OpenAI data centres was sharply scaled back, a commitment of credit rather than a company value, which is why [[money by kind|t-industry|v-money]] gives it a row of its own.

sections.name: Dev tooling & agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: MCP's roadmap, the AGENTS.md argument over agent configuration, and Go 1.27.
sections.lead: Agents need agreed interfaces, and two of this week's three items are about that: the Model Context Protocol published its roadmap, and a request for Claude Code to read the cross-tool AGENTS.md file became the week's argument over how agents are configured. Both are the plumbing under the [[harness theme|t-top|v-harness]]: a harness is the tools, context and rules around a model, and these are the formats it is written in. Go 1.27 shipped too. Cursor's Git hosting launch is in [[Top stories|t-top|i-cursor-origin]].

sections.name: Talk of the town
sections.label: Talk of the town
sections.glance: What to learn when models code, open-weight models doing real jobs, and Anthropic's watermarking in Claude.
sections.lead: What people argued about. Whether a 17-year-old should learn to build LLMs from scratch, against the worry that leaning on AI stops expertise forming; open-weight models doing real jobs, with GLM-5.3 rooting a tablet after four paid models failed and Qwen 3.8 27B as the local model of the moment; and whether watermarking Claude's text is acceptable. The open-weight thread continues in [[Models|t-models|i-ox-alpha]], where the stealth model Ox Alpha turned out to be GLM-5.3-Flash.

followups.html: Z.ai open-sourced the model and named it GLM-5.3-Flash: a mixture of experts with 320 billion parameters, 18 billion active, a 1-million-token context and up to 131,072 output tokens. OpenRouter had hosted Ox Alpha free without naming its developer ({{SiliconANGLE|https://siliconangle.com/2026/08/26/z-ai-open-sources-ox-alpha-model-as-glm-5-3-flash/}}).

followups.t: Nvidia buys Hugging Face for $12.93 billion
followups.html: First reported on Aug 26 as close to agreed at $12.9 billion ({{TechCrunch, Aug 26|https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/26/nvidia-closes-in-on-hugging-face-acquisition/}}, via {{the next issue|n:3cd5c17b0d0d81bba144e6734bb2fc8f}}), then confirmed on Sep 3 at $12.93 billion, just under the $13B+ offers reported in this issue. Jensen Huang said Hugging Face stays an open platform and Nvidia compute will not be required. The rejected Nvidia offer is dated "last year" in this piece and "earlier this year" in the Aug 24 one ({{TechCrunch, Sep 3|https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/03/nvidia-confirms-it-will-buy-hugging-face-for-12-9-billion/}}).

OpenAI launched GPT-6 Sol (and GPT-6 Luna) at $2 per million input and $10 per million output tokens, "down by half" from the 5.6 tier, with 90% discounts on cached input reads; OpenAI says it makes "about half as many mistakes" as GPT-5.6 Sol ({{MacRumors|https://www.macrumors.com/2026/09/22/openai-gpt-6-sol-luna/}}).

followups.t: The experimental vision model is retired
followups.html: DeepSeek's vision guide now says deepseek-flash accepts images, the name deepseek-v4-flash-vision-exp is still accepted but the model is retired, and the cap per image is 1,024 tokens (large images resized to about 1300 x 1300 pixels); the 600-image limit is unchanged ({{DeepSeek docs, read 2026-10-02|https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/vision/}}).

The CS-4 page now says more than 1,000 tokens per second on models exceeding 50 trillion parameters, where the Aug 19 version said 10 trillion ({{current page|https://www.cerebras.ai/cs4}}, {{archived Aug 19|https://web.archive.org/web/20260819141348/https://www.cerebras.ai/cs4}}). No source explaining the change was found.

followups.t: Harness scaling keeps going: Prime Agent and JIT-Agent
followups.html: The next issue reported Prime Intellect's {{Prime Agent|https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23552}} (Aug 24, open source) taking ARC-AGI-3 RHAE Best@1 from the same 30% baseline to 95.5% with a persistent IPython REPL, recursive subagents and versioned prompts, memories and skills, and {{JIT-Agent|https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25593}} using a 27B model to synthesise a task-specific harness, gaining 7.7 to 8.8 average points across nine agent benchmarks at 14.9 to 54.1% lower cost ({{2026-08-31: tech news|n:3cd5c17b0d0d81bba144e6734bb2fc8f}}). Figures as that issue reports them; not re-checked against the papers here.

glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: The first weekly digest of the knowledge base, covering roughly 2026-08-17 to 2026-08-24: 33 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools and the week's arguments, each with its sources. This tab is the week in one screen; every section has its own tab with the items in full.
glance.theme: The week's theme: the harness, not the model. Nvidia's AVO harness took Claude Opus 5 from 30% to 100% on ARC-AGI-3's public set, and the StateM runtime lifted every model it wrapped on Terminal-Bench 2.1, without touching the weights. Both put state, checks and memory outside the model; the [[animation in Top stories|t-top|v-harness]] runs the same task with and without them.
